tagline: Two high passes and a moving mountainside between former mining camps.
intro: The Silver Thread follows Colorado 149 through the San Juan Mountains, crossing the Continental Divide at Spring Creek Pass and climbing higher at Slumgullion Pass. Colorado DOT gives this 117-mile drive three hours and highlights the old mining camps, North Clear Creek Falls and the Slumgullion earth slide. The U.S. Secretary of Transportation designated it a National Scenic Byway in 2021.

Highway 149 was established in the 1920s and was not completely paved until 1977. Automobile visitors began arriving in Lake City around 1920, and their numbers grew as western Colorado highways developed and Hinsdale County roads improved. The scenic byway later extended north from Lake City to Blue Mesa Reservoir at the junction of US 50 and CO 149. The shift in travel had older roots: Lake City first served as a supply center for miners, while tourism became a viable industry there by the 1930s.

Starting at US 50, drive south past the edge of Curecanti National Recreation Area and the turn near Powderhorn, then follow the Lake Fork upstream to Lake City. Climb across the Slumgullion Earthflow to Slumgullion Pass, then cross Spring Creek Pass toward the upper Rio Grande. Continue through Creede and Wagon Wheel Gap to South Fork, where the highway meets US 160.

moments.title: Slumgullion Earthflow
moments.text: Slumgullion is a landslide in two stages: an older mass and a second flow moving over it. About 700 years ago, the first earthflow descended the valley and blocked the Lake Fork of the Gunnison River, creating Lake San Cristobal. The second flow has moved continuously for about 300 years, advancing about 23 feet a year over older, stable material. Highway 149 crosses the earthflow area southeast of Lake City. The U.S. Geological Survey investigated the natural dam and concluded that it is stable, citing its non-porous composition and a spillway partly cut into bedrock.

moments.title: North Clear Creek Falls
moments.text: North Clear Creek spills over Nelson Mountain tuff, rock formed from volcanic ash. The ash came from an eruption in the San Juan volcanic field about 27 million years ago. The creek is a tributary of the Rio Grande, and the falls lie within the Rio Grande National Forest. An overlook with a parking area and short trail sits about half a mile from Highway 149 on a paved county road. The overlook provides a view of the waterfall, and another trail leads to the top of a nearby bluff.
moments.notice: The waterfall drops over a deck of hardened volcanic ash.

moments.title: Wagon Wheel Gap
moments.text: Wagon Wheel Gap was the first tollgate on the journey between South Fork and Lake City. In the 1870s it served as both stage stop and supply town, beside the Rio Grande. Railroad magnate William Jackson Palmer began bringing visitors to the hot springs and providing lodging in 1883. He built a bath house at the turn of the century. The gap lies on Highway 149 at 8,468 feet, southeast of Creede. Nearby fluorspar mines operated from 1911 to 1950, adding mineral extraction to the history of a place used for travel and bathing.
